content: Iodine enters the food supply primarily through targeted interventions, with the most common method being the addition of iodine to food-grade salt, which is predominantly composed of sodium chloride. Women of reproductive age are particularly vulnerable to iodine deficiency, as their iodine-deficient neonates are at high risk of irreversible mental impairment. Breastfeeding women are another high-risk group, as breast milk may be the sole source of iodine for infants during their first six months of life. Globally, 88 billion people are at risk of insufficient iodine intake if iodine supplementation programs are not maintained. Approximately one-third of the global population resides in areas with naturally low iodine levels, necessitating permanent iodine supplementation strategies. An estimated 8% of school-aged children worldwide, or 241 million, have inadequate iodine intake, with the highest numbers in the WHO South-East Asia and African regions. Salt iodization is the preferred strategy for controlling iodine deficiency disorders and is implemented in over 120 countries. Many nations have successfully eliminated or significantly reduced iodine deficiency disorders through salt iodization and dietary diversification. Dairy products can also serve as a good source of iodine if cattle are fed iodine-enriched feed, making the inclusion of milk and dairy products in diets important for preventing iodine deficiency. The most visible sign of iodine deficiency is goiter, an enlargement of the thyroid gland. Inadequate iodine intake can impair the thyroid gland's ability to produce sufficient thyroid hormones, leading to hypothyroidism, which can damage the developing brain and cause a range of iodine deficiency disorders. The spectrum of iodine deficiency disorders includes goiter, hypothyroidism, increased susceptibility to nuclear radiation, spontaneous abortion, stillbirths, congenital anomalies, perinatal mortality, endemic cretinism (characterized by mental deficiency, mutism, spastic dysplegia, squint, hypothyroidism, and short stature), infant mortality, impaired mental function, delayed physical development, and iodine-induced hyperthyroidism. These disorders can be prevented by ensuring adequate iodine intake. However, both insufficient and excessive iodine intake can negatively affect thyroid function. Excessive iodine intake may lead to iodine-induced hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism, particularly in older adults with pre-existing nodular goiter. Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism is typically a transient condition that resolves with the correction of iodine deficiency. The recommended daily iodine intake varies by age and physiological status: 90 µg/day for infants and children under six years, 120 µg/day for children aged 6–12 years, 150 µg/day for adolescents and adults, and 250 µg/day for pregnant and lactating women. Dietary sources of iodine include sea fish, certain seaweeds, vegetables, cereals grown in iodine-sufficient soils, poultry, meat, and milk from animals consuming iodine-rich feed. Urinary iodine excretion (UIE) and urinary iodine concentration (UIC) are useful indicators for assessing iodine status, with a median UIC of ≥100 μg/L indicating sufficient iodine intake in adults. For pregnant women, a median UIC of <150 μg/L suggests insufficient iodine intake. The WHO has emphasized the importance of universal salt iodization since 1993, leading to significant progress in controlling iodine deficiency disorders. However, weak implementation of salt iodization programs in some countries remains a challenge. Excessive iodine fortification levels should also be avoided, as they may lead to excessive iodine intake. Salt iodization programs should be culturally appropriate, regulated by governments, and harmonized with other public health initiatives. Further research is needed to address gaps in evidence, particularly regarding the fortification of food-grade salt with iodine and its impact on iodine deficiency disorders.
